tagline.text: Forest ridges of Batangas and the Manabu traverse

location.label: Location
location.text: Talisay, Lipa City, Batangas · Santa Cruz, Santo Tomas City

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱1,500–3,500 (per person, with guide fee shared, transport included)

children.text: Mount Malipunyo is the highest peak of the Malepunyo (Malarayat) range spanning Batangas, Laguna and Quezon, a dormant volcano about 1,000 m high. The summit is a 3–5 hour climb from Talisay in Lipa, and the traverse on to Manabu Peak is also famous.

Mount Malipunyo (spelled Malepunyo in Wikipedia) is the highest peak of the Malepunyo range, which straddles the borders of Batangas, Laguna and Quezon in southern Luzon. The range is known as a dormant volcano (some sources say extinct) belonging to the Makiling–Malepunyo volcanic complex, with a caldera that opens to the south, lying between Lipa and San Antonio in Quezon. Wikipedia gives the highest peak as about 1,002 m while hiking blogs say around 1,005 m, so remember the summit as roughly 1,000 m. The area covers Santo Tomas, Lipa, Alaminos, San Pablo and Tiaong.
In the 1990s the same range was often called the Malarayat range, a name Wikipedia describes as erroneous (hiking blogs still use it as an alias). If Korean reviews or older hiking blogs say
Mount Malipunyo of the Malarayat range
, they mean the same mountain. Few peaks near Manila's south exceed 1,000 m, so people who have already done Mount Makiling or Mount Batulao often come here as the next step up.

The appeal of this mountain is the forest rather than the views. From the summit clearing you can see Mount Maculot, Taal Lake and Mount Makiling, but reports say the outlook is not wide open. Instead you get mossy trees and tangled vines, several ridge peaks, and streams, and the summit camp, with its cool evening breeze, is popular. The area is also known for alamid (civet) coffee, made from beans eaten and excreted by civets.

There are two main routes. The shorter climb from Talisay in Lipa to the summit is rated a minor hike at difficulty 3/9, while the traverse from the summit through Balete Peak and Biak-na-Bundok to Manabu Peak in Santa Cruz, Santo Tomas is rated a major hike at 5/9. Trails branch and are easy to confuse, so going with a local guide is practically standard. Fees and rules change every year, so check the latest information at the Talisay barangay outpost before you go.

blocks.title: Highest peak of a dormant volcano ridge

children.text: The summit of Malipunyo is the third of three peaks, about 1,000 m above sea level. A small cleared viewpoint sits at the top, facing Mount Maculot, Taal Lake and Mount Makiling. Early morning on a clear day is best.

blocks.title: A trail where the forest is the star

children.text: Reviewers agree that the forest, not the view, is the mountain's main attraction. Thick roots, vines and moss make the path pleasant even on dim days. In return, thorny plants and itch-causing lipa trees line the way, so you need long sleeves and pants.

This route runs from the summit through Balete Peak and Biak-na-Bundok to Manabu Peak (about 755 m). A 2019 group hike set off at 4:30 AM and reached the Santa Cruz exit around 3 PM, taking more than ten hours.

This side trail branches off early from Talisay, and round-trip times vary from 3 to 4.5 hours depending on the review. The path is unclear and rocky, so it is safer with a guide. One option is to leave your bags at the guide's house and go light.

It is breezy and cool at night near the summit, and the overnight itinerary camps near the top. Reports say the main route has only one water source, so people fill 3–4 liters there before climbing on.

blocks.title: Manabu Peak and Enkantierra Nature Park

children.text: On the Santo Tomas side, Santa Cruz has the Manabu trailhead and Enkantierra Nature Park. The Malepunyo Challenge trail run was held here on August 10, 2025, with 5 km, 10 km, 20 km and 32 km categories. Ordinary hikers use it as the traverse exit or as the start of the reverse route.

items.title: Day hike — Talisay in Lipa to the summit
items.subtitle: A light out-and-back climb

children.text: Leave Manila. Take a bus to Lipa or Batangas City and get off near Fiesta Mall in Marawoy. An early start from Manila is best.
Take a tricycle from Fiesta Mall to the Talisay barangay outpost. The distance depends on road conditions, so tell the driver to go to the outpost (barangay outpost).
Sign the logbook at the outpost and arrange a guide. The trails branch and confuse, so be sure to bring a guide.
Enter the forest path from the trailhead. About an hour later you pass a water source.
After 3–5 hours of climbing, reach the summit (Peak 3). Eat lunch and rest at the viewpoint clearing.
Head back down the same way. Some sections are slippery, so be more careful than on the way up.
Return to Talisay, take a tricycle into Lipa and board a bus back to Manila.
This timetable is an example based on blog records. Slower hikers should choose the two-day option, and plan so that you are back in the village before dark.

items.title: 2 days, 1 night — camp at the summit, descend to Atisan in San Pablo
items.subtitle: An overnight at the summit

children.text: Gather in Buendia, Alabang or Cubao in Manila and take a bus to Lipa.
Register at the Talisay outpost and start walking. About an hour later, fill your water at the source.
Arrive near the summit and camp. Nights get cool, so bring a windbreaker.
Break camp early and descend via Talahiban toward Atisan village in San Pablo.
Reach Atisan, travel to San Pablo for lunch, then take a bus to Manila from Lucena or San Pablo.
This descent route follows blog records from 2007 to 2015. Check locally whether it is still used.

items.title: Traverse — Malipunyo to Manabu Peak
items.subtitle: A serious hike of more than ten hours

children.text: Set out from Talisay in the dark and reach the summit, Peak 3. The 2019 account says dawn broke at the second peak.
From the summit, begin the traverse toward Manabu and pass Balete Peak.
Pass Biak-na-Bundok Peak and the section with the tree-house rest stop.
Reach the Manabu campsite and summit.
Descend to the Manabu trailhead in Santa Cruz, Santo Tomas, wash up and board your vehicle.
Actual reports took more than ten hours and included crawling sections and big rocks. You need to pace yourself, hike with a guide and bring a headlamp.

Take a bus from Manila (Buendia, Cubao, Alabang) bound for Lipa or Batangas City and get off near Fiesta Mall in Marawoy, Lipa. A 2015 blog lists ₱180–200 by bus or van from Manila to Batangas, and ₱125 by van from Pala-Pala in Dasmariñas, Cavite to Lipa.
Travel time from Manila to Lipa varies a lot with traffic, so allow plenty of time. These fares are old records, so confirm them locally.
Hiking clubs often rent a van, leave at dawn and return around lunchtime.

items.title: From Lipa to the Talisay trailhead

children.text: Take a tricycle from Fiesta Mall to the Talisay barangay outpost. The blog records mention a ₱150 ask, about ₱100 after bargaining, alongside an older ₱50–80 record.
Where the road turns rough, vehicles cannot continue and you have to walk. The 2019 group hike went by van to the end of the rough road and walked about 20 minutes to the entrance.
The Manabu trailhead in Santa Cruz, Santo Tomas City, has Enkantierra Nature Park. Go from Manila to Santo Tomas City by bus or private car, then use a tricycle.
From that side, Manabu Peak takes about 2 hours and the Malipunyo summit 7–9 hours.
For the traverse, it is best to send a private car from one trailhead to the other.

Batangas has a dry season from November to April. Trails are less slippery and streams are not swollen, making it a good time to hike. The forest is coolest from December to February, though morning fog is possible.

In the rainy season (June–October) it rains often, rocks and roots are slippery and thick fog makes it easy to lose the trail. The June 2019 group hike record also notes fog, rain and slippery ascents.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: Best hiking season. Dawn fog possible at the summit.
An early start is essential. Carry plenty of water.
Slippery and easy to get lost. A guide is a must.

There is no lodging on the mountain itself, and you camp near the summit. Lipa has restaurants and convenience stores around Fiesta Mall, and for a night at the foot of the mountain it is easier to use lodging in Lipa, Santo Tomas or San Pablo. Staying in town the night before and leaving at dawn makes a day hike much easier.

Eat in Lipa before the hike and bring your own lunch and trail snacks. Alamid coffee is known locally, so you can ask your guide whether it is available. There are no stores on the mountain, so carry all your trash back out.
A guide is practically essential. Several reviews say trails branch and confuse, and one group walked in circles for 17 hours.
Bring long pants and arm sleeves. Thorny plants (teka-teka, tingloy) and itch-causing lipa trees are common along the trail.
Fill 3–4 liters at the water source on the main route before climbing on. Water purification tablets or a filter are safer still.
Bring a headlamp and a power bank. If the traverse or descent runs late, you will walk after dark.
Records say phone signal reaches most of the course, but it varies by spot, so download maps beforehand.
An early start is best. Starting to walk from the village before 8 AM leaves you time to spare at the summit.
Stay with your group and match the guide's pace. Traverse reviews warn that going ahead alone and getting lost is dangerous.
Check the latest notices for entry rules and fees. I could not confirm the current exact entrance and guide fees on any official page.
This is a mountain where trails branch and people often get lost. Do not climb alone without a guide, and attempt the traverse only after checking your stamina and time.
Blog reviews mention snakes (one record says a guide was once bitten), wild boar and monkeys. Watch your footing near streams.
Touching lipa trees can cause severe itching. Do not grab unknown trees with your hands.
When it rains, rocks and roots are slippery and some paths run along cliff edges. In the rainy season it is safer to postpone.
At the end of the traverse there are crawling sections and big rocks to climb, which is dangerous if you arrive with no energy left.

Most of the fares and times here come from 2007–2019 blog records. I could not find official guidance from the last 12 months, so confirm with the Talisay outpost or the local governments (Lipa City, Santo Tomas City) before leaving.
A mountain on the western side of the same volcanic complex, suited to those who want something lighter than Malipunyo. Confirm distance and travel time locally.
A lake in San Pablo city proper, handy to visit after coming down toward Atisan. You can eat and rest nearby.
Taal Lake is visible from the summit in that direction, and after the hike you can continue on to Taal Volcano and the old Spanish town.
A mountain visible from the summit viewpoint and a popular trekking peak climbed from the Lipa and Tanauan side.
